Wind gusts recorded across the county were between 50 and 60 mph. A delayed report was received from an observer in Kit Carson, CO that a wind gust bent a 24-foot flag pole about 5 degrees and ripped the flag to pieces. This wind gust was estimated at around 80 mph based on damage.

Strong northwest winds moved across portions of Eastern Colorado with gusts ranging from 51 to 66 mph. The strongest winds were observed in the northern half of Yuma County, impacting the cities of Yuma and Wray. The combination of strong winds and dry fields produced areas of localized blowing dust with visibility reported as low as 2 miles during the early part of the afternoon.

Strong northwest winds moved across portions of Eastern Colorado with gusts ranging from 52 to 62 mph. The strongest winds were observed in the city of Burlington. The combination of strong winds and dry fields produced areas of localized blowing dust with visibility reported as low as 3.5 miles during the early part of the afternoon.
Strong northwest winds produced wind gusts up to 59 mph. The strongest winds were observed northwest of the town of Max, Nebraska.
Strong northwest winds moved across Hitchcock County producing wind gusts up to 79 mph. The strongest wind gusts were measured in Trenton, Nebraska.

Strong northwest winds moved across Hitchcock County producing wind gusts of 55-69 mph. The strongest wind gusts were measured in McCook, Nebraska where there were also localized reports of blowing dust with visibility as low as 5 miles due to the dry soil conditions.
Strong northwest winds gusted from 51 to 59 mph during the afternoon hours with the strongest gusts measured in St. Francis, Kansas.

A combination of dry soil conditions and high winds gusting up to 59 mph produced localized areas of blowing dust during the afternoon hours across the county. Visibility ranged from 7 miles to near zero at times.

Strong northwest winds gusted from 59 to 70 mph during the afternoon hours with the strongest gusts measured near Edson, Kansas. With a combination of the wind gusts and dry soil conditions, localized blowing dust produced visibilities as low as 5 miles near Goodland, Kansas.

Several bands of light to moderate snow moved generally south across Dundy County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 5 to 6 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulations were located near the town of Parks, Nebraska.  Key impacts:  snow packed roads.

Several bands of light to moderate snow moved generally south across Hitchcock County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 6 to 8 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulations were located near the towns of Trenton and Stratton, Nebraska. At times, the snowfall rate was heavy enough with winds gusting up to 30 mph to produce reduced visibility to a few miles. Key impacts:  snow packed roads, blowing snow.

Several bands of light to moderate snow moved generally south across Decatur County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 3 to 6 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulations were located near the town of Norcatur, Kansas.  At times, the snowfall rate was heavy enough to produce reduced visibility to around three-quarters of a mile.

Several bands of light to moderate snow moved generally south across Norton County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 4 to 8 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulations were located near the city of Norton, Kansas.  At times, the snowfall rate was heavy enough to produce reduced visibility to around half a mile. A damaging quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) tornado moved across Sharon Springs, Kansas during the late evening/overnight hours of April 22nd, 2022. Maximum winds were found to be around 110 mph, which makes this tornado an EF-1, just short of an EF-2. The worst damage was noted at the KDOT station near Highway 40 where a cinder block building was toppled and a truck shed was completely destroyed, as well as the CHS facility where the office building had its roof completely torn off. Throughout town, there were many tree limbs broken, tree trunks broken, and trees uprooted. Many buildings and vehicles had broken windows. Power poles were broken or downed throughout town. Other damage included several rolled trailers (ag-related, RVs, or work trailers), fences blown down, shingles off roofs, and other wind-related damage.

A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) tornado formed in far northern Sheridan County before crossing into southern Decatur County. Damage consisted of highway signs down and/or twisted, a tree trunk was snapped, a few blown over irrigation pivots, and a railroad crossing gate was destroyed.

A train travelling near the town of Parks created sparks on the tracks that created a grass fire of unknown size between the railroad and mile markers 15 to 16 along U.S. Highway 34. Multiple fire units from nearby towns and counties, including an air fire support plane, assisted with putting the fire out over a span just over 7 hours. The fire caused a small portion of Hwy 34 around mile markers 15 and 16 to be closed for a few hours while crews worked to put it out. No structures or equipment were damaged by the fire.

A significant snow band produced extreme impacts across central Kit Carson County. Snow totals ranged from 7 inches near Burlington and around 6 inches in the western part of the county to well over a foot in the central part of the county. In fact, several reports of over 12 inches were received, with the highest being a measured 18 inch snow depth in Stratton, CO. Interstate 70 was closed from Limon, Colorado to Goodland, Kansas around 2 pm MDT as a result of the wintry conditions. There were some reports of snow drifts as well. Finally, agriculture impacts were reported in the form of calves being buried in the snow drifts and some perished as a result of the heavy snow. Key impacts: heavy snow, snow drifts, agriculture/cattle losses, transportation delays, road closures.

A long duration light snowfall event was experienced across Sherman County. In addition, a heavy snowband that formed earlier in the day across eastern Colorado moved into the extreme northwest portions of the county. Snowfall across Sherman County ranged from around 2 inches in the east to 6 inches reported north of Ruleton, or the northwest corner of the county. In addition, Interstate 70 was closed from Limon to Goodland as a result of the extreme snow amounts reported over eastern Colorado, but roads across Sherman County were also reported to be snowpacked. Key impacts: light to moderate snow, transportation delays, road closures.

A significant snowband impacted Yuma County, and more specifically southern and eastern Yuma County. Amounts ranged from around an inch in far northwestern Yuma County to 10 or higher inches across southern Yuma County. The highest amounts reported were 9.5 inches in Wray, Colorado, but with amounts over a foot reported in far northern Kit Carson County, it's quite possible storm totals approached one foot along the southern Yuma County border, between the Joes/Kirk area and Highway 385. Some snow drifts were also observed with this event. Key impacts: heavy snow, snow drifts, transportation delays, road closures.

A heavy snowband produced impactful snow across portions of Cheyenne County. The highest measured report received was 6 inches at a location six miles north of Wild Horse. However, based on radar imagery and the slow movement of the heavy snowband, it is likely that higher amounts would have been reported in central Cheyenne County, particularly north central Cheyenne County. Amounts likely exceeded 8 inches in this area, but could have been 12 inches based on reports from central Kit Carson County. There were also some snow drifts observed with this event. Key impacts: heavy snow, snow drifts, transportation delays, road closures.

WSR 88D confirmed a tornado debris signature in northern Logan County that eventually crossed into southern Thomas County. Upon further review and information/video gathered, it was determined that a tornado moved across extreme southern Sheridan County. This tornado was confirmed by damage from NWS Storm Survey, tornado chaser video, and a brief/weak tornadic debris signature on NWS Goodland WSR 88D radar imagery. Damage consisted of several large healthy tree limbs snapped, one treat snapped near the base, and a power pole down. Based on the damage, maximum wind speed was determined to be 100 mph.

A significant wildfire, which began in Decatur County, Kansas and moved into Furnas County, Nebraska, eventually crossed into Red Willow County, Nebraska. The fire primarily burned across rural eastern Red Willow County, but it did cross over Highways 6/34 in the northeastern part of the county, as well as Highway 89 in the southeastern part of the county. A multi-mission aircraft from Colorado mapped the fire and showed it to have burned an area 28 miles long across 44,024 total acres, putting the number of acres burned in Red Willow County at around 28,000, with 15,000 in Furnas County, NE and 1,000 in Decatur County, KS also burned. Resources from all over were deployed to help with this fire, including 3 Nebraska Air National Guard Blackhawk Helicopters and a Type 1 National Incident Management Team. Total personnel exceeded 100 at times. In addition, a NWS Incident Meteorologist (IMET) was deployed to this fire, the first deployment of an NWS IMET in our forecast area's history. Fighting the fire was difficult due to the rural/terrain area it was in, as well as persistent blowing dust. One fatality occurred with this fire as a retired fire chief was overcome by smoke and fire after the vehicle left the road on Friday, April 22nd during conditions of poor visibility from smoke and dust. An additional 5 injuries were also reported with fire fighters battling this blaze. Temporary evacuations were issued for Bartley and Indianola.

A significant wildfire began in Decatur County, Kansas and moved into Furnas and Red Willow Counties in Nebraska. The fire was confined to the far northeastern part of the county as it started here and quickly burned north-northeast. A multi-mission aircraft from Colorado mapped the fire and showed it to have burned an area 28 miles long across 44,024 total acres, putting the number of acres burned in Decatur County around 1,000 acres, with Red Willow County at around 28,000 and 15,000 in Furnas County, NE. Resources from all over were deployed to help with this fire, including 3 Nebraska Air National Guard Blackhawk Helicopters and a Type 1 National Incident Management Team. Total personnel exceeded 100 at times. In addition, a NWS Incident Meteorologist (IMET) was deployed to this fire, the first deployment of an NWS IMET in our forecast area's history. Fighting the fire was difficult due to the rural/terrain area it was in, as well as persistent blowing dust.

The rear flank downdraft caused damage in several locations on highway 83, including grain bins at a feed lot and outbuildings at a farmstead.

This tornado caused two injuries, including the driver of a vehicle which was thrown off Interstate 70, and an older male attempting to get into his storm cellar when he was struck by flying debris.

Strong winds blew down a powerline that caused a grassfire. The boundaries of wildfire were CR Kiowa to CR Rawhide (S to N) and CR 130 to CR 170 (W to E). Roughly 2248 acres were burned in the fire. No injuries, no livestock hurt, and no damaged structures were reported as the fire stayed in grassland and canyons. Highway 25 was closed due to the smoke and the fire. Wallace, Logan, Greeley, and Wichita fire departments responded to the fire.

A strong low pressure system moved northeast over East-Central Colorado generating seven hours of blizzard conditions across Yuma County. There were numerous reports from the public, along with the Wray and Yuma AWOS stations, of visibilities dropping to between a quarter mile to zero miles. Winds were out of the west-northwest with gusts up to 48 mph. During the event, up to eight inches of snow fell with drifts reportedly up to seven feet tall in spots. Key impacts: blowing snow, snow packed roadways, heavy snow, and blizzard conditions.

A strong low pressure system moved northeast over East-Central Colorado generating heavy blowing snow across Yuma County. There were numerous reports from the public, along with the Wray and Yuma AWOS stations, of visibilities dropping to between a quarter mile to zero miles during blizzard conditions. During the event, snow amounts ranged from a trace to eight inches across the county with drifts reportedly up to seven feet tall in spots. The greatest snow accumulations occurred along and north of Highway 34 near the city of Yuma. Key impacts: blowing snow, snow packed roadways, heavy snow, and blizzard conditions.

A strong low pressure system generated roughly 7.5 hours of blizzard conditions across Kit Carson County. Winds were out of the northwest with gusts up to 62 mph recorded. The strongest gust was observed via the Kit Carson County Airport ASOS station in Burlington, Colorado. The high winds were observed from 10:18 AM MT through 12:45 PM MT. The only damage reported from the high winds was a broken window in Flagler, Colorado. Visibility reductions ranged as low as one-quarter mile to near zero across the county. Snow amounts ranged from one to three inches. Key impacts: blowing snow, snow packed roadways, and blizzard conditions.
KITR ASOS reported non-thunderstorm wind gusts over 58 mph during this time with a maximum wind gust of 60 mph at 2:39 PM MST.

A strong low pressure system moved northeast across East-Central Colorado into Northwest Kansas generating three hours of blizzard conditions across Cheyenne County. There were numerous reports from law enforcement and the Cheyenne County Emergency Manager of visibilities dropping to between a quarter mile to zero miles, mainly along Highway 36. Winds were out of the west-northwest with gusts up to 40 mph. During the event, up to three inches of snow fell with drifts reportedly up to three feet tall in spots. Key impacts: blowing snow and blizzard conditions.

A strong low pressure system moved northeast across East-Central Colorado into Northwest Kansas generating four hours of blizzard conditions across Sherman County. There were numerous reports from an off-duty NWS Employee of near blizzard to blizzard conditions in the city of Goodland, Kansas, with visibilities dropping to between a quarter mile to near-zero miles. Winds were out of the west-northwest with gusts up to 60 mph. The high winds occurred from 11:45 am MT to 12:41 pm MT. During the event, up to three inches of snow fell with drifts reportedly up to three feet tall in spots. Key impacts: blowing snow, high winds, and blizzard conditions.

A strong low pressure system moved northeast across East-Central Colorado into extreme Southwest Nebraska generating three hours of blizzard conditions in Dundy county. There were several reports of visibilities dropping as low as one-quarter mile mainly near the town of Haigler, Nebraska. Winds were out of the northwest with gusts up to 44 mph. During the event, up to three inches of snow fell across the county, with the greatest accumulation over the western half of the county. Key impacts: blowing snow and blizzard conditions.
A wall of dust was seen on radar and satellite moving through Rawlins County. Surrounding counties reported 0.25 mile or less visibility.
A wall of dust was seen on radar and satellite moving through Decatur County. Surrounding counties reported 0.25 mile or less visibility.

Although no gusts of 50 knots or greater were recorded, surrounding counties reported high wind conditions. There is reason to believe Decatur county reached high wind conditions even though there were no direct observations of that occurring.

The highest snow accumulation was reported at 2 miles north-northwest of Kirk, Colorado. At times, the snowfall reduced visibility to around three quarters of a statute mile. U.S. Highway 36 was reported closed from the Kansas/Colorado border to the Yuma/Washington county border due to the snow. Key Impacts: heavy snow, transportation delays, road closures.

Light to moderate snow fell across Kit Carson County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 4 to 7 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulation was reported at 13 miles southwest of Joes, Colorado. At times, the snowfall reduced visibility to around a half of a statute mile. Interstate 70 was reported closed from the Kansas/Colorado border to the Kit Carson/Lincoln county border due to the snow. Key Impacts: heavy snow, transportation delays, road closures.

Light to moderate snow fell across Sherman County producing total snow accumulations ranging from 2 to almost 5 inches across the county. The highest snow accumulation was reported at 13 miles north-northwest of Ruleton, Kansas. The Kansas Highway Patrol reported an accident on Interstate 70 about two miles east of Kanorado, Kansas involving an automobile striking the rear of a semi truck at 4:50 AM MST due to the hazardous driving conditions caused by the the winter weather. The accident resulted in one person seriously injured and transferred to the nearby medical center. Two people were also reported uninjured in the accident. Key Impacts: automobile accidents, transportation delays, road closures.

At 10:10 AM on the 18th, the public reported 8 inches of snowfall since the start of the storm. The night before, at 8:40 PM, law enforcement reported 0.12 inches of freezing rain that was causing hazardous travel. The highest snowfall report of 12 inches was received from the public at 7:15 PM on the 18th. Winds at both the Yuma and Wray AWOS sites reported gusts over 20 mph which resulted in blowing snow. The blowing snow reduced visibility under 1 mile on occasion. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads and icy roads.

Near 1:40 AM on the 18th, the Colorado Department of Transportation closed Interstate 70 through Kit Carson county due to safety concerns. A maximum snowfall report of 10 |inches was sent in by the public 7 AM on the 19th. Multiple reports across the county had reports of over 6 inches of snow from this event. The Burlington ASOS reported gusts up to 37 mph during the winter storm while it was snowing. Reduced visibility down to 0.5 mile due to blowing snow at the ASOS site, however it is likely that lower visibilities occurred and were not reported. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

An observer in the southwestern portion of Dundy county reported 9 inches of storm total snowfall on the morning of the 19th. Farther east in the county, snowfall totals were around 4 inches. Winds between McCook, Nebraska and Wray, Colorado were gusting over 25 mph for majority of the storm. These winds caused blowing snow that reduced visibility. The McCook ASOS reported visibilities down to 0.25 mile multiple times during the event and it is likely similar conditions were experienced in Dundy county. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

In the northeastern portion of the county, the public reported 8 inches of snow on the morning of the 19th as a storm total. Another report of 7.5 inches was recorded in the far southern portion of the county. Snowfalls tapered off in the western half of the county with totals around 3-4 inches. Winds between McCook, Nebraska and Wray, Colorado were gusting over 25 mph for majority of the storm. These winds caused blowing snow that reduced visibility. The McCook ASOS reported visibilities down to 0.25 mile multiple times during the event and it is likely similar conditions were experienced in Dundy county. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

In the northeastern corner of Red Willow county, the public reported 12 inches of snow on the morning of the 19th as a storm total. Another report of 11 inches was received from the west-central area of the county. Most of the county seems to have received over 6 inches of snow from the storm. Winds at the McCook, Nebraska ASOS occasionally gust to 30 mph and frequently over 25 mph during the storm. These winds caused blowing snow that reduced visibility. The McCook ASOS also reported visibilities down to 0.25 mile multiple times during the event. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

On the morning of the 19th, the public reported 8 inches of storm total snowfall in the south central portion of the county. This was the highest amount of snowfall reported in Cheyenne County with other locations near the center of the county reported around 4 inches of snow. The AWOS in St. Francis reported multiple gusts over 20 mph which created blowing snow reducing visibility down to 0.25 mile at times. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

On the morning of the 19th, an observer reported 8 inches of storm total snowfall in the northeast portion of the county. This was the highest amount of snowfall reported in Cheyenne County, with other locations reporting 4 to 6 inches of total snowfall. The CWOP near Atwood, Kansas reported multiple gusts over 20 mph which created blowing snow that reduced visibility. Key impacts: heavy snow, blowing snow, snow packed roads.

Over a period of 27 hours, Yuma County experienced freezing fog, freezing rain, and heavy snow. During the day on the 2nd, the fog produced visibilities as low as one-quarter mile with moisture from the fog and following freezing rain creating ice accumulations up to 0.08 inches. The greatest ice accumulations occurred near Wray, Colorado. During the evening hours through the early morning hours on the 3rd, heavy snow produced two to six inches of snow over the county. The highest snow amounts were reported on the west side of the county in and near the town of Yuma, Colorado. Key impacts: reduced visibility, heavy snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Over a period of 27 hours, Kit Carson County experienced freezing fog, freezing rain, and heavy snow. During the day on the 2nd, the fog produced visibilities as low as one-quarter mile with moisture from the fog and following freezing rain creating ice accumulations up to 0.02 inches. The greatest ice accumulations occurred near Burlington, Colorado. During the evening hours through the early morning hours on the 3rd, heavy snow produced two to six inches of snow over the county. The highest snow amounts were reported on the west side of the county near the town of Flagler, Colorado. Key impacts: reduced visibility, heavy snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Over a period of 18 hours, Logan County experienced freezing fog, freezing rain, and light to moderate snow. During the day on the 2nd, the fog produced visibilities as low as one-quarter mile with moisture from the fog and following freezing rain creating ice accumulations up to one-quarter inch. The only reports of ice accumulation came from city of Oakley, Kansas. During the afternoon to evening hours, light to moderate snow produced one to five inches of snow over the county. The highest snow amounts were reported in the northeast corner of the county in the city of Oakley. Snow drifts up to a foot were also observed. Key impacts: reduced visibility, heavy snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Over a period of 24 hours, Cheyenne County experienced freezing fog, freezing rain, and light to moderate snow. During the day on the 2nd, the fog produced visibilities as low as one-quarter mile with moisture from the fog and following freezing rain creating an unknown amount of ice. During the afternoon to overnight hours, light to moderate snow produced three to five inches of snow over the county. The highest snow amounts were reported in Saint Francis. Key impacts: reduced visibility, snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Over a period of 22 hours, Rawlins County experienced freezing fog, freezing rain, and heavy snow. During the day on the 2nd, the fog produced visibilities as low as one-quarter mile with moisture from the fog and following freezing rain creating ice accumulations up to 0.20 inches. The greatest ice accumulations occurred along Highway 36 between Atwood and Herndon. During the evening hours through the early morning hours on the 3rd, heavy snow produced three to eight inches of snow over the county. The highest snow amounts were reported in the northeast side of the county near the town of Ludell, Kansas. Key impacts: reduced visibility, heavy snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Over a period of nearly 24 hours, Dundy County experienced heavy snow. The highest snow amounts were reported in the northern half of the county near the town of Parks with reports of four to eight inches across the county. Key impacts: heavy snow, and hazardous travel conditions.

Snow squall. A band of heavy snowfall extending across portions of East-Central Colorado moved east-northeast across Yuma County over a span of an hour. The snow squall created visibility reductions as low as one-quarter mile mainly near the city of Yuma with reports up to one inch of snow. Key impacts: visibility reductions, hazardous travel, heavy snow.

Snow reports of a trace were received; however, due to the blowing snow it was difficult to take measurements. Key impacts: visibility reductions, hazardous travel.

Snow squall. A band of heavy snowfall extending across portions of East-Central Colorado moved east-northeast across the Kansas border and Sherman County over a span of 45 minutes. The snow squall was dissipating as it moved over Sherman County, creating visibility reductions as low as a quarter mile in the western part of the county along I-70.  However further east at Goodland the visibility improved to three-quarters of a mile that mainly impacted travel across I-70. Snow reports up to one inch of snow were reported. Key impacts: visibility reductions, hazardous travel.

Snow squall. A band of heavy snowfall extending across portions of East-Central Colorado moved east-northeast across the Kansas border and Wallace County over a span of roughly one hour. The snow squall was dissipating as it moved over the county, creating visibility reductions as low as three-quarter to one-half mile that mainly impacted travel across US Highway 40. Snow amounts up to one inch were estimated. Key impacts: visibility reductions, hazardous travel.

Snow squall. A band of heavy snowfall extending across portions of East-Central Colorado moved east-northeast across the Kansas border and Greeley County over a span of two hours. The snow squall was dissipating as it moved over the county, creating visibility reductions as low as one-half mile that mainly impacted travel across the county. Snow reports ranged from three-tenths up to one inch of snow were reported. Key impacts: visibility reductions, hazardous travel.

The river gauge 4 miles east of Clayton remained at or above flood stage for 21 hours due to heavy rainfall during the late afternoon and evening of May 22nd. Low land flooding occurred along Prairie Dog Creek leading to Sebelius Reservoir.  An unattended camper floated away when the waters rose.

Heavy rainfall from two separate storms on June 4th resulted in continued minor flooding in town overnight and the following morning with some roads remaining impassible. All reservoirs and ditches remained at capacity during the morning of June 5th before the water slowly receded after the reservoirs were pumped out.

Emergency manager reported Highway 34 and 61 were both closed due to flash flooding. Highway 34 was closed from Benkelman to Trenton while highway 61 was closed from Benkelman to Enders. Up to 8 feet of water over the road was reported by Fire and Rescue. At least one car and driver were stranded in the water and a secondary road was completely washed out. The eastern portion of Dundy county remained largely under water for the following days.

Highway 61 remained closed until at least the evening of the 28th when water was still 3 or more feet deep over the road between Benkelman and Enders. Highway 34 between Benkelman and Trenton also remained closed due to flood waters of an unknown depth. Of the parts of the highways and other county road that were starting to be above water on the 28th, washouts and other damage were reported.

In around around Stratton, at least one home and multiple cars were being swept away from flash flooding. Water rescues were required to save at least 4 citizens inside their homes. The town of Palisade also had extensive flooding but to less of an extent than Stratton. Highway 34 from Benkelman to Trenton was closed due to flooding. Highway 25 from Trenton to highway 6 was also closed.  The first report of flash flooding was when a driver became stranded near Palisade and needed rescue.

Highway 34 from Benkelman to Trenton was closed due to flooding. Highway 25 from Trenton to highway 6 was also closed. The train bridge west of Stratton was washed out due to the flooding. A road grader was also found to be almost fully submerged.
The Frenchman creek was reported to be out of its bank and flooding county multiple roads, although it seemingly never flooded over highway 6.

Barnett Park in McCook flooded due to the Republican River rising out of its banks. It remained flooded until the afternoon of the 28th. Highway 34 and 83 both had to be closed due to the river flooding over them.

In the afternoon of the 26th, the waters had stopped rising, but the town of Herndon was cutoff by all land routes until the late morning of the 27th, when all but one road became traversable. Multiple county roads were also submerged for days later, however on the 30th, flooding conditions subsided and no more roads were reported underwater, although there were many that had been washed out and destoryed.

At 8:35, dispatch reported multiple roads under water in Herndon. Over the following hours, conditions worsened dramatically. The town of Herndon became completely cutoff and surrounded by flood waters. These flash flood waters also put a levee upstream of the town to become at risk of failing, which would have flooded the town. Thankfully, the levee held and was able to be reinforced in the afternoon hours. North of Ludell, at least one country road culvert was completely washed out, making the road impassable.

This is an estimated snow depth from the totality of the event. Interstate 70 was closed off and on for multiple days due to the heavy snow before fully opening Saturday afternoon. Key impacts: heavy snow, visibility reduction, and road closures.

A public report in the town of Kit Carson reported 12 inches of snowfall for the duration of the event, along with four inches of precipitation in the rain gauge. Additional reported snowfall amounts ranged from 1 to 5 inches, with 5 inches of snowfall falling from the start of the event through at least 9:17am MST 15.6 N of Haswell. Another report of 4 inches of snow fell on November 8th alone 14 SSW of Wild Horse.  Key impacts: heavy snow and visibility reduction.

Snow began in Yuma county during the early morning of November 6th and continued through the early morning on November 9th. The greatest reported snow amount was 13 inches 2 ESE of Yuma, which was for the duration of the event. Additional snowfall reports ranging from 3-12 inches were reported. Other reports of 12 inches for the event were reported from Kirk and in the town of Yuma as well. Eight to ten inches of snow fell in Wauneta from the 6th through the 8th along, with 7-9 inches of snow in Wray during the same time period. Nearly all state highways across the county were closed at some point during the event. Key impacts: heavy snow, visibility reduction, and road closures.

The greatest storm total for this event was 26.9 inches 13 SW Joes in northern Kit Carson county. Additional snow reports in excess of 2 feet were reported in Flagler, 15 S Stratton and 9 SSW Joes. Additional amounts ranging from 6 to 18 inches of storm total snow was also reported across the county. There was a report 1 WSW of Burlington of a partially collapsed car port, tree limbs broken from the heavy snow as well. Interstate 70, and nearly all other highways, were closed at some point during the event. Interstate 70 first closed during the day of the 6th and then reopened that night and then closed again this time for a prolonged period from the morning of the 8th through the afternoon of the 9th. Key impacts: heavy snow, visibility reduction, and road closures.

Spotter reported street flooding and basements being flooded in Yuma.  Pictures from other sources show hail accumulating to around a foot deep.  The combined affects of deep hail and heavy rainfall likely overwhelmed the storm drains, preventing the heavy rainfall from draining away.  Unclear how many basements were flooded, or how much damage was caused by the flooding.

The Goodland ASOS regularly reported gusts between 58 and 67 MPH between 12:30 and 15:00 LST. Starting about about noon LST, the main front began moving into Sherman county meaning gusts around 58 MPH may have occurred earlier than the official start time of 12:30, but no supporting observations have been found. Tailing the front by about 5-20 minutes were convective showers. An initial increase of winds occurred with the front, but the tailing storms allowed stronger, more widespread winds to mix to the surface. Around 1400 LST, convection cleared the county, but the Goodland ASOS continued reporting gusts up to 67 MPH until 1500 LST. The convectively driven winds and wind damage reports will be included as Thunderstorm Wind gusts.

A wall of dust formed along the cold front that was advancing across the east half of the county.  Loose soil from a field near I-70 added to the dust in the air. Tornado formed south of farmstead near River Road, made a glancing blow to the farmstead, then continued NNW toward Hwy 36.  Power poles were broken, a well established cotton wood tree was uprooted, and a well anchored antenna was twisted and bent by the tornado. Another farmstead north of CR M was also impacted by the tornado. The tornado removed the roof and doors from a metal building, relocated a couple grain bins, and leveled a wooden shed. However the tornado turned away from house before continuing north through the windbreak.  The tornado ended before reaching the highway.
An off duty NWS Employee reported a tornado roughly 7 miles north of Kanorado. Pictures of a funnel and a dust swirl was also passed along as well.  No damage occurred.
Storm survey pictures of a hay wagon with partial bale in it was tipped to the north. A smaller metal bin was thrown as well. An electric fence was also completely destroyed as well.

Continuation and ending of track coming out of Scott County. This tornado destroyed oil an oil battery near Little Jerusalem Park, and damaged items at the park entrance that were bolted into concrete.  Strength taken from DDC survey. Track estimated from rotation on radar, arial photos, and the few damage reports that were received.

A significant tornado developed south-southwest of Grinnell west of the CR S and 22 intersection, then moved north-northeast across I-70 and over the western four blocks of the town of Grinnell before dissipating in a wheatfield north of the Grinnell Cow Paddy Golf Club.  The tornado caused damage to farmstead at CR X and 26, and east of the CR Z and 26 intersection.  Damage included moving round bales, leveling wooden sheds, pushing farm equipment and vehicles, and breaking large tree limbs.  Roughly 40 houses in Grinnell were damaged or destroyed, along with quonsets or other sheds.  Notable damage included moving a house roughly four inches off the foundation, debris piercing the grain bins on the north side of town, causing thousands of bushels of grain to spill out, complete destruction of a house built in the 1800s, and moving a couple graveside head stones a couple hundred yards.
Continuation of the Gove County tornado that impacted Grinnell.
Part of a irrigation pivot was tipped over.

The same supercell which produced Grinnell tornado produced another EF3 tornado in Sheridan County, which led to damage to portions of a homestead. The worst damage was broken bolts and metal brackets of a metal frame that was bolted into concrete.  The tornado also removed the roof from a barn nearby, as well as leveling a cinderblock garage and removing/destroying wooden and metal grain bins.  The tornado started just northwest of CR 110 S and 40W based on Sentinel satellite data, crossed CR 90 S and 80 S, then lifted just northwest of County Road 406 and CR 20 W intersection based on the same Sentinel data as well.

Based on damage and satellite footage, a second corridor of damage occurred northwest of the homestead. The damage tracks of the two tornadoes merge at the end point of this tornado. This tornado twisted a pivot, broke several power poles, and removed tree tops from the west edge of the windbreak.

The tornado touched down south of Muddy creek where it tore shingles off of a house. The tornado then traveled to the north and crossed Road 714.  As it crossed the road it completely removed a metal machine shed, which included pulling bolts through the concrete foundation.  The structure was tossed roughly 50 yards to the north.  Other notable damage at this location included leveling two buildings at an old farmstead, pushing a combine roughly 60 feet, tipping over an empty grain cart into a grain truck, pushing a drill backward in the shape of a quarter circle, and then scattering seven empty cattle feeders feeders in a line going north into a wheat field.  ||The tornado continued north to CR 717 where it damaged trees and grain bins, broke a power pole, and blew a stock tank over a hundred yards at a homestead.  The tornado then turned northeast crossing 12th Ave and CR 720 causing damage to trees, pivots, or structures.  It then turned back north after passing the CR 720 and Veteran's Highway intersection.  It continued along Veteran's Highway, breaking off 30 power poles before ending just south of a homestead between CR 723 and CR722.  ||The path north of CR 714 is estimated based on radar imagery and connecting the points of the tornado damage that was surveyed.

Yuma county emergency manager relayed that multiple fires were ongoing across the county as wind gusts of 60-83 mph were ongoing behind a cold front. There were also three smoke plumes on radar as well. The largest was named 33 Fire as it was along CR 33 near the town of Heartstrong, Colorado. It is believed the fire was started from downed power lines from the wind. The fire burned 12,000 acres but with the only damage known to be to an abandoned trailer and a pig barn with no livestock inside. The other fires from that day burned around 2000 acres near CR L in Yuma county and 50 acres near CR 44. Near the intersection of CR T and 28 a 15x20 chicken building with 20 chickens, 9 ducks and 1 rabbit was lost along with some minor damage to a goat pen. Fire damage was also reported to sprinklers and fence line near the intersection of CR 27 and CR U. A vacant house was burnt down as well near the same intersection.

At least two residences sustained major damage, and many others significant damage, as an intense thunderstorm moved over northeast Yuma county. Several large grain bins were destroyed with others damaged.  One grain bin fell on a parked semi-trailer causing additional damage to the vehicle.  Ten irrigation sprinkler systems was overturned, numerous trees were uprooted. Window and siding damage occurred at several residences with parts of roofs damaged.  Y-W electric reported a loss of 44 utility poles.  In addition, thousands of acres of cropland were impacted by the hail accompanying the storm.  Dollar estimates of damage are approximate and based on figures from the USDA.
Golf ball to hen egg sized hail was reported along with thunderstorm wind damage.

A couple of traffic signs were blown down in town.  Just south and west of the intersection of U.S. 83 and U.S. 40, an irrigation sprinkler was overturned, a grain bin was buckled in and loosened from its mounting, and about 10 utility poles were broken.

A small thunderstorm complex produced a long-swath of significant wind and hail damage across south-central into central Wallace county.  The damage began near the Wallace-Greeley county border about 13 miles SSW of Sharon Springs, and continued to about 8 miles SSE of Wallace.  Approximately 25 irrigation pivots were blown over, numerous grain bins were either damaged or destroyed, utility poles were broken, some outbuildings damaged and one semi-truck blown over. Some residences reported shingle damage and broken winds due to a combination of wind and hail.
The hail was mostly the size of golf balls, but the largest was baseball sized.  The hail lasted for about ten minutes.  Windows were broken due to the combination of large hail and strong wind.

Many streets in Hoxie have at least six inches of water flowing over them due to persistent heavy rainfall.

The worst damage occurred in northern Graham County just east of Highway 283.  Storm chasers reported at least one satellite tornado rotating around this main tornadic circulation.

This large tornado moved from northern Graham County into Norton County, dissipating near Norton County Road E-6 and Highway 9 west of Densmore.  The tornado was still producing EF2 damage in Norton County as it destroyed utility poles, grain bins and tree rows.  A farmstead suffered significant damage west of Densmore.  The roof was heavily damaged, vehicles and farm implements were moved, with grain bins and outbuildings damaged or destroyed.

Prolonged heavy rainfall occurred over Red Willow County, mainly southeast of McCook.  Radar estimates of four to ten inches rain fell, with the highest amounts east of Highway 83 between Highways 89 and 34.  Highway 83 was closed in McCook due to flood waters causing vehicles to stall and become abandon on the highway.  Numerous other roads were also reported to be closed.    McCook was the only town in the county affected by the flooding.  No specific property damage information from the flooding was given.

Repeated rounds of moderate to heavy rainfall continued over the flood area into the overnight hours.  Highway 83 was closed due to stalled vehicles being stalled and abandoned on the highway.  Numerous other roads were also closed due to the flooding.  No specific information was given regarding property damage.
Hail was accompanied by estimated wind gusts of 50 MPH.

The North Fork of the Solomon River was out of its banks causing all of Lenora to be flooded, along with a stretch of Highway 9 coming into town as well as elsewhere in the southern part of the county.   Swift water rescues occurred in the southern part of Norton county during the late evening of the third.  One of these rescues involved a couple who under estimated the depth of the water over the highway and drove through the flood waters on Highway 9.  The vehicle was washed off the road and caught in a tree.  The couple escaped from the vehicle and climbed into the tree, remaining there until rescuers arrived.  There was one direct fatality from the flooding.  The individual was driving north from Graham County on county roads toward Lenora.  He drove into flood waters, under estimating their depth.  His vehicle was washed off the road.  His body was found a quarter mile away from the vehicle.  In general, the majority of the rainfall fell south of CR W.  Rainfall amounts of five to seven inches were common across southern Norton County.  No information was given for property damage.

As of 2 PM CST water is still covering many roads and bridges in the south part of the county.  Prairie Dog Creek and the North Fork of the Solomon River continue to be out of their banks.  No information was given for property damage.

Bow Creek in the north part of the county is out of its banks.  There is extensive flooding of county roads in the north part of the county, with an estimated seven inches of water over the roads early in the event.  Water is covering Highway 283 in several locations in the northern part of the county, with debris floating across the highway.  No report was given for property damaged by flooding.

Around sunrise campers at Antelope Lake reported flood waters up to the steps of their camper, almost covering the tires.  Estimated the water to be at least a foot deep.  Roads in southern Norton County, where similar amounts of rain fell, were reported to still covered in water by mid afternoon.  Using this report as a proxy, roads in northern Graham County were likely to still be covered by flood waters for a similar period of time.  No information was given for estimates of property damage.
The bridge north of Jennings was reported to be underwater the following morning due to heavy rainfall from the nighttime.  No damage was reported.

The blizzard conditions were over the east half of the county.  Twenty people had to shelter in place in Bird City.  A day after the storm there were still many power outages across the county.  An estimated 3-4 inches of snow fell over the southeast part of the county and melted quickly. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

White-out conditions were observed just north of Goodland.  A peak wind gust of 60 MPH occurred at 525 AM MST.  The blizzard conditions were mainly east of Highway 27.  Snowfall totals were close to 20 inches along the east border of the county, with amounts declining to the west.  During part of the blizzard Goodland lost power. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Near zero visibility reported across the county.  The entire county was without power.  Some had receive power the day after the storm, but many were still in the dark.  Many wrecks, slide-offs, and rescues were reported.  Snowfall totals ranged from 8 to 28 inches, with the highest snow amount in Wallace. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Visibility of a block was reported in Horace.  All highways were closed across the county due to poor driving conditions.  KDOT is waiting to clear the roads until conditions improve, and has contacted the National Guard to help.  Motorists were rescued from seven vehicles stranded near Tribune.  Most of the county is without power.  Snowfall amounts close to 30 inches were reported. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Atleast three inches of snow per hour were occurring near Herndon.  Near zero visibility was reported near Herndon and near Atwood.  Cedar trees 50 ft. tall 7 NW of Atwood had lost almost all of their branches, with diameters of the limbs ranging from 6-8 inches.  A dead tree standing for 67 years with a diameter of four and a half feet fell over.  Power is out for many across the county, with some still without power the day after the storm.  Four people were rescued from stranded cars, 40 people had to shelter in place in Atwood.  Fifteen inches of snow was reported 8 SSE of Atwood, with potentially a few more inches toward the southeast part of the county.  Snowfall amounts declined to the northwest, with almost no snow reported over the far northwest corner of the county. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Visibility of less than 75 feet was reported in Colby.  A peak wind gust of 64 MPH was reported 2 ENE of Colby at 426 AM CST.  The very strong winds and heavy, wet snow split a tree in half in the center of Colby.  The largest limb that broke was eight inches in diameter.  A warming center was opened overnight with occupants then moved to hotels afterwards aided by the Red Cross.  Power outages were reported in Colby, Rexford, and Brewster.  The day after the storm Colby had power again.   The National Guard in Thomas County had two of their four hummers stuck in the snow, causing them to restrict their rescue to stranded motorists who had medical problems. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Blizzard conditions were reported in the Oakley area, with whiteout conditions reported outside of town. In Oakley tree branches from two to nine inches in diameter, and one eight inch diameter tree, were blown down from the weight of the snow and the strong winds.  Snowfall reports ranged from 26 inches 6 E of Wallace to 14 inches near the Gove County line. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

Blizzard conditions were reported 11 N of Leoti along with no power since 3 AM CST.  Between 20 and 30 inches of snowfall occurred across the county. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

One over the northeast part of the county and one over the south. A federal disaster was declared by President Donald J. Trump.

The Colorado State Climatologist measured the hailstone using a set of calipers to get the exact measurement to the hundredth of an inch. The hailstone measured 4.83 inches in diameter at its widest point. The home owner commented that the hailstone was brought indoors and secured in a freezer approximately 30 minutes after falling due to safety concerns from ongoing severe weather. Despite social media pictures taken soon after the hailstone had fallen, which were higher than the 4.83 inch measurement, the official diameter measurement is 4.83 inches. The hailstone weighed 8.5 ounces, its widest circumference was 12.875 inches, and its volume was later measured using 3D imagery at 16.549 cubic inches.

Hitchcock County Emergency Management reported a tornado south of Culbertson, NE. The tornado crossed Highway 17 between mile markers 10 and 11. No damage was reported and no clear damage was found by NWS storm survey on May 18th, 2019.

The tornado began just south of Highway 34 along the Red Willow and Hitchcock County line. The tornado moved north-northeast across Red Willow County before ending northwest of McCook, NE. The tornado struck a farm and this is where the most intense damage was done. Otherwise, damage consisted of sporadic tree  limbs down, some barbed wire fences knocked over, irrigation pivots overturned, and minor loss of metal roofing.||The primary damage occurred when the tornado moved across a farm. The tornado entered the property from the southwest, where it went through a wind break and snapped numerous hardwood and softwood trees. The storm also destroyed 6 grain bins, 5 farm outbuildings, and produced significant damage to a house. The EF-2 rating is a direct result of the house damage, which consisted of a few collapsed exterior brick walls, uplift or removal of half of the structure's roof, and complete removal of the garage. Additional damage included shattered windows to the house and vehicles, damage to a combine due to being struck by a grain bin, damage to fences, and other trees with losses to branches.

As the heavy rainfall expanded west, so did the flooding.  Highway 34 was closed from the state line west to Wray due to flooding.  The ball fields on the east side of Wray were also flooded. There was plenty of erosion/damage along the edges of the Republican River. There were also lots of basements flooded (around 15-20 significantly). Damage from the flood waters is unknown at this time. One thing the Wray City Manager wanted to be noted was that there are 6 flood control dams on the south side of the town. These worked perfectly and slowed the water. Had the system failed, the flooding damage would have been much worse.

Areal pictures show the flooding mainly confined to the Republican River valley continuing well into the daylight hours.  Fields were flooded along the river, as well as water running over roads.  Anything in Wray along the Republican River was flooded.  This included parks, buildings, and some streets that didn't have a large capacity for drainage underneath.  Based on footage during the daytime, Highway 34 west out of Wray did not have water over it.  Damage from the flooding is not know at this time.

A strong front moved southeast across Sherman County producing winds with gusts between 55-80 mph. In northern Sherman County, up to 70 mph wind gusts were observed for a duration of one hour and 50 minutes. These strong winds snapped an 8 inch diameter tree limb off a fruit tree and another tree to fall, which crushed a fence, in Goodland. The Goodland ASOS observed a peak gust of 66 mph during the event. The high winds also caused blowing dust to occur, which reduced visibilities between one mile to a few hundred yards.

As a strong cold front moved across Sherman County, strong winds ranging from 27 to 80 mph caused dirt to be lifted into the air. The blowing dust reduced visibilities between one mile to a couple hundred yards.

A strong cold front moved southeast across Greeley county producing high winds ranging from 40 mph to 60 mph. The peak gust of 60 mph was observed north of the town of Tribune. These high winds lifted dirt into the air at least one thousand feet above ground and reduced visibilities between one-quarter mile near Horace to two blocks in Tribune.

Blowing dust associated with a strong cold front caused reduced visibilities of less than one hundred yards on Highway 83 in southern Decatur County. The nearby mesonet stations were observing gusts between 40-50 mph around the time of the report.

A strong cold front moved southeast across Gove County producing high wind sustained at 30 to 55 mph with gusts from 59 to 62 mph for a duration of 15 minutes. The wind gusts were measured via a mesonet station near I-70 in the northeast corner of the county.

Strong winds associated with a strong cold front lifted dirt and corn leaves into the air. The blowing dust caused reduced visibilities between one-quarter mile to near-zero on Old Highway 40 between Grainfield and Grinnell. Nearby stations have missing observations, so the wind gusts are unknown.

As a strong cold front moved southeast across Norton County, dirt was lifted in the air. The blowing dust caused reduced visibilities from fifty to ten yards near the town of Norton. A strong cold front moved southeast across Norton County producing high winds. At the time of frontal passage, many mesonet stations and the AWOS have inaccurate or missing observations. The first observation reported by the Norton AWOS was at 7:55 pm CDT with a gust of 64 mph.

A strong cold front moved southeast across Graham County producing high winds sustained at 40 to 69 mph with gusts ranging from 58 to 81 mph. The Hill City ASOS station recorded a 66 mph peak gust. A mesonet station northeast of Bogue recorded a peak gust of 81 mph. During the event, Graham County Dispatch reported the high winds downed power lines which sparked a few sporadic fires around the county and cut power to the ASOS station after the 7:40 pm CDT observation. A more notable fire on south and southeast of Nicodemus due to the embers from a trash burning fire catching the grass on fire. No injuries or structural damage was reported from the fires. The high winds also lifted dirt into the air which caused reduced visibilities in Hill City of one hundred to two hundred yards. At 7:21 pm CDT, a car accident occurred due south of Hill City on Highway 283 due to the reduced visibilities. No injuries were reported.

A strong cold front moved slowly southeast across Graham County producing wind gusts ranging from 58 to 81 mph. The high winds lifted dust high into the air, which caused reduced visibilities as low as two hundred to one hundred yards in Hill City. These reduced visibilities caused one accident on Highway 283. No injuries were reported.

As a strong cold front moved across Graham County, high winds gusted between 59 to 81 mph. Around 7:13 pm CDT, Graham County dispatch received a report of an out of control trash burning fire that was burning fields near the historic town of Nicodemus. The fire was close enough to town that the entire town was evacuated for a few hours as thirty five firefighters and 15 trucks responded from multiple counties to stop the fire. The Graham County Fire Department reported the fire was 1.5 miles wide and 2 miles long. The fire occurred to the south and southeast of Nicodemus and extended south to K-18 and east to the Rooks County line. Around 9:30 pm CDT, dispatch reported the fire had moved into Rooks County and was mostly under control or out completely. No injuries or structural damage was reported.

Multiple bands of snow produced up to 2 inches of snow. The snow accumulated on roads, creating slick conditions that caused several vehicle slide-offs on I-70 and Highway 24. One non-injury accident involving a passenger vehicle was reported at 4:21 PM MST on December 28th located at mile marker 448 on I-70. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple bands of snow produced light snow accumulations across Cheyenne County ranging from 1 to 2 inches. At 6:58 pm CST on December 28th, a semi-truck traveling north-bound on KS-27 near the Kansas-Nebraska state line slid at the base of a hill due to snow-packed roads. The semi blocked both lanes of traffic for four hours with police units from Dundy County, Nebraska and Cheyenne County, Kansas responding to the situation. No injuries were reported. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple bands of snow produced up to 2 inches of snow across Sherman County. Roads became snow-packed during the event, resulting in numerous slide-offs. The slide-offs most often occurred along US-24, KS-27, and I-70. Sherman County dispatch reported a passenger vehicle accident on the Kanas side of the Colorado-Kansas state line at 7:30 pm MST on December 28th. No injuries were reported. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple snow bands moved across Thomas County producing snow amounts of 2 to 3.7 inches. The highest snow totals occurred in the northeast corner of the county with 3.7 inches of snow reported near Rexford. Numerous slide-offs were reported during the event, particularly on I-70 and US-83. On December 28th, two accidents were reported with no injuries. At 6 pm CST, a semi-truck and a passenger vehicle collided near mile marker 60 on I-70. At  9:52 pm CST, a passenger vehicle slide off the road and into a ditch on County Road 31 half a mile off US-83. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple snow bands moved across Wichita county, producing only a trace of snow. While snow accumulations were low, roads became slick. At 8:07 am CST on December 29th, a passenger vehicle accident was reported on KS-25 near mile marker 118. One person was injured. Key impacts: traffic accident.

Multiple bands of snow moved across Logan County during the event, producing a range of snow from a trace to 1.8 inches. The Logan County Emergency Manager also reported freezing drizzle that accumulated a glaze of ice on surfaces. Several slide-offs occurred on I-70 along with two accidents. At 7:49 pm CST on December 28th, a rollover accident occurred on US-40 between County Roads 360 and 370 with a passenger vehicle containing five passengers. Three injuries were reported. At 11:36 pm CST on December 28th, a 2 passenger vehicle collision occurred on I-70 near mile marker 79. No injuries were reported with the second accident. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple bands of snow moved across Gove County producing a range of snow amounts from a trace to 2 inches. Numerous slide-offs were reported on I-70 and KS-212. At 5:28 pm CST on December 28th, a rollover accident involving a passenger vehicle occurred near mile marker 99 on I-70. No injuries were reported. At 6:05 pm CST on December 28th, a two semi-truck collision occurred resulting in one injury and a truck stuck in a ditch. The accident occurred near mile marker 99 on I-70. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Snow amounts across Yuma County ranged from a trace to 2.5 inches. The highest amounts of snow were found near the city of Wray. Two accidents were reported along US-34. The first accident was a passenger vehicle in Yuma, while the second was a passenger vehicle five miles east of Yuma. Key impacts: traffic accidents.

Light snow accumulated across Sherman County ranging in amounts from 1 to 2 inches. Two accidents with no injuries occurred near the Colorado-Kansas state line on I-70 around 6:15 am MST. A passenger vehicle spin-out also occurred on I-70 near mile marker 31 around 6:20 am MST due to slick roads. No injuries were reported. Key impacts: traffic accidents.

Shortly before midnight the very strong winds stirred up embers from a fire four and a half miles northwest of town that had burned out weeks ago.  The winds directed the fire southeast toward Benkelman.  The fire grew larger as it headed southeast.  Shortly after 3 AM MST the assistant emergency manager issued an evacuation order for Benkelman due to the fire continuing to move toward town.  The smoke from the wildfire was thick enough to drop the visibility to near zero in some spots.  The evacuation order was lifted at 7:30 AM MST.  The fire was stopped on the northwest edge of Benkelman where part of the fire had jumped Hwy 34.  There were some isolated spots in the northwest part of town as far as two blocks away from the fire that were burned from embers of the wildfire.  A restaurant near where the wildfire was stopped had extensive smoke damage, as did the high school.||The only building that was burned was a small outbuilding near a motel on the northwest side of town.  A total of sixteen fire trucks helped put the fire out.||Key impacts:  wildfire.

During the afternoon hours on the 14th, rain gradually transitioned to snow across Kit Carson County as a surface cyclone moved across the area into western Kansas. The full transition to snow occurred after sunset and became heavy at times, with the greatest accumulations occurring in the western half of the county.  Snow accumulations ranged from a trace near Burlington to 7 inches north of Flagler.  This snow as an additional amount from the lighter snow accumulations that occurred in the western half of the county on the evening of the 13th. A trained spotter near Flagler reported an estimated 10 inches from the 13th to the 15th. Key impacts: Slick roadways, heavy snow, reduced visibilities.

During the late afternoon hours on the 14th, rain gradually transitioned to snow across Yuma County as a surface cyclone moved across the area into western Kansas. The full transition to snow occurred after sunset and became heavy at times, with the greatest accumulations occurring in the southwestern corner of the county. Wet snow accumulations ranging from a trace near Idalia to 3.5 inches in Joes were produced during this event. A CO-OP observer reported  3 inch diameter tree limbs had broken off trees due to the weight of the snow. Other tree limbs were reported to be leaning. Key impacts: Slick roadways, moderate to heavy snow, reduced visibilities, damage to trees.

A large, multi-vortex tornado moved across northwestern Sheridan County, Kansas, impacting the town of Selden. The tornado started west of town initially and moved slowly to the east, eventually crossing Highway 83. As the tornado crossed the highway, it started to impact structures on the west side of Selden, and eventually moving across the town. In town, damage was widespread and quiet concentrated. At one point, the tornado reached a width of one half mile wide. Damage consisted of thousands of broken tree limbs, hundreds of uprooted and snapped trees, shingles off and pieces of roofing removed from residences and buildings, many farm outbuildings either missing roofing material, walls damaged, and/or the building completely collapsed and removed from its foundation, windows broken out of houses, buildings, and vehicles, snapped power poles, overturned irrigation pivots, overturned semis and rail cars, and several grain silos blown over.||The tornado then proceeded to the east, exiting town and heading towards the Highway 83 and Highway 383 split. There were a few more irrigation pivots overturned, as well as power poles snapped. The tornado appeared to dissipate as it neared the Highway 83 and Highway 383 split due to a lack of any visible damage at that intersection.||The challenge with this survey was there were multiple vortices causing damage. Therefore, there were a few areas of more concentrated high-end EF-1 damage with broad/widespread EF-0 to EF-1 damage.||There was one minor injury with this event. The town tornado sirens were not functioning as a result of a power outage. Therefore, fire fighters jumped into their vehicles to drive through town to warn people of the coming tornado. Powerlines fell upon one of the trucks, striking a fire fighter in the back of the neck. Injury was treated on scene.

A brief tornado occurred 5 miles north of Benkelman. Damage consisted of some metal roofing panels, a shed was thrown 200 yards, and fencing was damaged. The tornado crossed Highway 61 and ended on the west side of the highway. There was a distinct break in the tracks between this tornado and the EF-2 that began a few minutes later.

An EF-2 tornado occurred shortly after the brief EF-0 north of Benkelman. Damage consisted of many broken power poles, a large grove of Elm Trees that were demolished, additional trees that were snapped or uprooted, damage to a residence including loss of shingles, loss of metal roofing panels to a farm outbuilding, a tractor was moved 100 yards, and damage to antique vehicles due to falling tree debris. The tornado moved along Highway 61 for most of its life, snapping more power poles and twisting signs. The tornado seemed to stray slightly west of the highway and continued according to spotter and chaser reports. The tornado eventually ended over open fields.

A tornado hit a farmstead northwest of Herndon. At the farmstead, damage consisted of numerous snapped and uprooted trees, several farm structures damaged including torn off metal roofing, broken windows, and even a few metal support beams bent in. Several grain silos were damaged or removed from their foundation. Windows were broken in vehicles. A house suffered damage to shingles, a few broken windows, and a tree falling onto it. The tornado then proceeded north on County Road 27, snapping power lines and damaging a refurbished farmstead schoolhouse. As the tornado moved north, it also damaged some oil storage tanks, spreading the oil to the northeast in a field as it turned. The tornado crossed the field, and a damage path was observed on County Road 29. From there, there was no observable damage so it was determined the tornado ended at this location.

Intense straight line winds due to the microburst first occurred at 8:12 PM MDT near the Burlington airport. This began an area of intermittent damage consistent with wind speeds in the 100-115 mph range. The most intense winds occurred over an area 4.2 miles long and 600 yards wide, ending near Interstate 70 and the Kit Carson Correctional facility. The most significant damage occurred near the Burlington airport where a large evergreen tree was snapped at the trunk and near the Kit Carson Correctional Facility where four power poles were snapped and a nearby outbuilding was destroyed. Damage due to winds in the 60-80 mph range continued to the north of Interstate 70. Additional storm damage included: uprooted trees; damage to the wind and visibility sensors of the KITR ASOS, a camper trailer, overhead garage doors (blown in/dented), fences, windows, siding and roofs of outbuildings and a mobile home; and the flipping of shipping containers and semi-truck trailers. The city of Burlington also lost power as a result of the storm damage.

A portion of the metal roof of a Dollar General store in Saint Francis was peeled back allowing daylight to be seen from customers inside the store near a wall of the building due to winds estimated to gust up to 90 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Decatur County. Mesonets across the county recorded wind gusts of 59-73 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Oberlin, Kansas. There was damage to a power pole that caused loss of power in Oberlin and damage to an unknown number of roofs across the county due to estimated gusts up to 100 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Gove County with mesonet stations recording high wind gusts of 58-88 mph, with the peak gust located near Gove, Kansas. The Gove County Emergency Manager reported multiple outbuildings destroyed across the county, one trailer home rolled, and five roofs were ripped off in the city of Quinter. The winds estimated to cause this amount of damage was up to 110 mph.

Two rounds of high winds moved across Graham County with mesonet stations recording high wind gusts of 58-81 mph, with the peak gust located in Hill City, Kansas. There was extensive damage across the county due to the high winds. One barn was blown down onto a roadway, six outbuildings were destroyed. Two homes were damaged in the county with one home considered abandoned. Older structures, including barns, around the county received various degrees of damage, mainly to the old tin roofs. There was also an unknown number of power poles down/leaning around the county. An unknown number of trees also sustained damage during the event, with one report listing 3.5 to 4 inch diameter tree limbs ripped off an evergreen tree in Hill City. With the degree of damage across the county, winds are estimated to have gusted up to 110 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Greeley County over a period of four hours. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 59-70 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Selkirk, Kansas. Several outbuildings were destroyed  while numerous powerlines and trees were reported down across the county. In the southeast corner of the county, near Selkirk, one home had it's roof blown off. West of the city of Tribune, the top of a metal elevator bin was blown off, also damaging the stairwell for the bin. North of Tribune, a shed and a shop were knocked down due to the high winds. Given the degree of damage observed across the county, the wind gusts were estimated to be up to 110 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Logan County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded peak wind gusts of 69 to 84 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Oakley, Kansas. There were an unknown number of outbuildings destroyed and broken windshields across the county. Other damage due to the high winds include the collapse of the landfill fence, an old roof and siding were torn off an old barn, and a shop had half the roof blown off. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 100 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Norton County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-90 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Lenora, Kansas. In the city of Norton, high winds caused the rear wall of a two-story building to partially collapse. Near the town of Densmore, half a tin roof was torn off an old barn with the wooden support beams caved inside. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 120 mph.
Two rounds of high winds occurred across Rawlins County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-84 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Atwood, Kansas.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Sheridan County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-70 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located north of the town of Tasco, Kansas. Several outbuildings were blown down across the county; however, the most significant damage occurred in Hoxie where the metal roof was torn off a chiropractor's office. Other noticeable damage in Hoxie included a Jeep window blown out in Hoxie. Near Campus, Kansas, a power pole was cracked, multiple tree limbs of an unknown size were down, and the roof on an old farm house was nearly gone. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 110 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Sherman County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-81 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located in Goodland, Kansas. Numerous trees, power poles, and power lines were reported down across the county with power outages reported in Caruso and Goodland. In Goodland, high winds damaged stop signs, road signs, a wooden chest acting as a flower bed, a section of wooden fencing at two residences, and collapsed a metal mailbox inward towards the center while remaining on it's stand. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 100 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Thomas County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-81 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located in Colby, Kansas. Numerous power poles and lines were reported down across the county. The town of Rexford lost power due to the high winds. On I-70 near Levant, a semi truck was blown over due to high winds at mile marker 43. In Colby, numerous trees had various sized limbs down or were uprooted and a pivot irrigation system was knocked over. There were also reports of shingles blown off roofs and two windows broken on a vehicle parked in a strip mall parking lot. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 110 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Wallace County. Mesonets across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-87 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Sharon Springs, Kansas. There was a range of damage across the county, but mostly in Sharon Springs. Up to 6 pivot irrigation systems were blown over along with a portion of corral and pasture fencing. Up to 8 power poles were damaged, 4 in Sharon Springs. Additional damage included Christmas decorations blown away, fencing blown over, a carport, and the tin roof of a house. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 100 mph.

Two rounds of high winds occurred across Wichita County. Mesonet stations across the county recorded wind gusts of 58-83 mph, with the strongest recorded gust located near Leoti, Kansas. Across the county there were numerous trees down, 2 of which fell on houses in Leoti. A barn was blown down in Coronado and Wichita County High School in Leoti sustained roof and structural damage. There were also various degrees of roof and shingle damage across the county. The wind gusts capable of this degree of damage were estimated to be up to 110 mph.

High winds knocked over a power pole in a corn field, sparking a fire along County Road N south of Cheyenne Wells. The fire burned 125 acres, damaging an irrigation pivot and burning an unknown number of power poles near the field.

High winds knocked over a powerline which sparked a wildfire in the northeast corner of Gove County that gradually moved into southeast Graham County near the community of St. Peter, Kansas. This fire burned approximately 4,520 acres damaging several outbuildings and grassland. The Gove-Sheridan-Graham fire burned a path length of roughly 9 miles across the three counties.

High winds knocked over power lines near the towns of Marienthal and Lydia, sparking two large fires. The fire near Marienthal began around 14:30 PM CST burning fields and one home. The Marienthal fire burned approximately 1200 acres and was put out around 22:30 PM CST. The Lydia fire began around 13:50 PM CST burning fields, two homes, and several vehicles over a span of 8300 acres. This fire injured one non-hospitalized person and another person died the next day due to burns and a collapsed lung from protecting his home. The Lydia fire was extinguished around 22:06 PM CST.

High winds knocked over power poles in Gove County sparking two large fires. The first fire started around 13:32 PM CST roughly 5 miles northeast of Quinter near the Gove-Sheridan-Graham county line. This fire burned approximately 1500 acres of wildlife and grassland area in Gove County. Damage included numerous burned down trees and power poles. The Gove-Sheridan-Graham fire burned a path length of roughly 9 miles across the three counties. The northeast Gove fire was extinguished around 18:00 PM CST in Gove County, but continued to burn in Sheridan and Graham counties.||The second fire began around 14:04 PM CST and was approximately 12 miles southeast of Gove where it burned another 1500 acres of land. This wildfire burned several storage structures, two grain bags, fenceline, a limestone building, wheat fields, along with numerous power poles and trees. This fire was mostly extinguished during the late night hours; however it continued to have hot spots until roughly 14:00 PM CST on the 17th.

High winds, very low relative humidity, and thick blowing dust created static electricity that interacted with pasture fencing approximately 10 miles east of Russell Springs beginning around 13:58 PM CST. This fire burned mostly crop land and fencing over 3200 acres. The fire was roughly six miles wide spreading from County Road 370 to County Road 410. Due to the magnitude of the event, there was no end time provided for this specific fire.

High winds knocked over power poles in northeast Gove County sparking a wildfire that traveled into extreme southeast Sheridan County near Sheridan Lake beginning around 13:40 PM CST. The Gove-Sheridan-Graham fire burned a path length of roughly 9 miles across the three counties, with one of those miles in Sheridan County. The fire burned roughly half a mile wide in Sheridan County damaging grassland, crop land, and trees along a creek bottom near Sheridan Lake. Due to burning trees and tall grass, the fire continued to burn into the next day, with fire crews leaving the area around 16:00 PM CST on the 16th. The fire continued to smolder for a week.  The Gove-Sheridan-Graham fire burned a path length of roughly 9 miles across the three counties.
